title: 4B. Taxonomic composition (track B: insects)
text:
Compare the relative abundance of insect groups across habitats, months and extraction methods.

Select samples
We use the matched samples selected in step 3 throughout this analysis. semi_join() keeps only their rows in the counts table, without loading the full table into R:
selected <- duckdb_tibble(eventID = samples$eventID, .prudence = "stingy")
counts_selected <- merged$counts |> semi_join(selected, by = "eventID")


Sum reads by taxonomy
We use sum_clades_long() from step 2 to aggregate reads at a chosen taxonomic rank, then add habitat, month and extraction method:
get_composition <- function(rank) {
  composition <- sum_clades_long(counts_selected, merged$asvs, ranks = rank) |>
    as.data.frame()
  merge(composition, samples[c("eventID", "habitat", "month", "method")], by = "eventID")
}
Available ranks are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species and otu.


Plot taxonomic composition
The function below selects the most abundant taxa across all selected samples and plots their mean share of reads for each habitat, month and extraction method using ggplot2.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, top_x = 10) {
  composition <- get_composition(rank)

  # Absent taxa have no rows, so a mean is the sum divided by the number of samples
  totals <- tapply(composition$norm, composition$clade, sum)
  top <- names(sort(totals / nrow(samples), decreasing = TRUE))[1:top_x]

  monthly <- aggregate(norm ~ clade + habitat + method + month, composition[composition$clade %in% top, ], sum)
  n_samples <- aggregate(eventID ~ habitat + method + month, samples, length)
  monthly <- merge(monthly, n_samples)
  monthly$share <- monthly$norm / monthly$eventID

  # Reversed levels put the most abundant taxon at the bottom of each bar
  monthly$clade <- factor(monthly$clade, levels = rev(top))
  monthly$month <- factor(monthly$month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)
  monthly$habitat <- factor(monthly$habitat, levels = names(habitat_cols))
  monthly$method <- ifelse(grepl("homogenate", monthly$method), "homogenate", "lysate")

  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))

  ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = share, fill = clade)) +
    geom_col(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.2) +
    facet_grid(habitat ~ method) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(mycols(top_x), top), breaks = top, name = rank) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean share of reads") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}


Example: plot top orders
Plot the eight most abundant orders:
plot_barplots(rank = "order", top_x = 8)
Each row is a habitat, with the homogenate samples on the left and the paired lysate samples on the right. Each bar shows the mean relative abundance of these orders among samples from a given habitat, month and method. Flies (Diptera) dominate the reads, especially in alpine habitats and early in the season. Bars may not add up to 100% because only the eight most abundant orders are shown.
These are shares of sequencing reads, not estimates of the number of individuals or biomass. Empty months indicate that no selected samples were available in that habitat.
Consider: How does taxonomic composition vary across habitats and seasons? Could differences in read abundance reflect factors other than the abundance of organisms?
Discuss: How do the homogenate and lysate protocols differ? Which insects would you expect each method to favour, and does the plot support this?

title: 2B. Data preparation (track B: insects)
text:
Load and combine the insect data in long format, and summarise read counts by taxonomy.

How the data look

ASV read counts can be organised in wide format, with one row per ASV and one column per sample, or in long format, with one row per ASV–sample combination. The tables below show the same read counts in the two formats.


Wide

sample 1

Long

ASV a
251






This track uses long format, as delivered by the ASV portal. It omits the many zeros and works well with database tools, so we can analyse the large insect datasets without loading them into R.



Load the datasets
We use two tools to work with large datasets without loading everything into R:

Parquet is a file format for storing data efficiently on disk.
DuckDB lets us analyse these files without loading the entire dataset into R.

Load the data from the data_path folder defined in the previous section:
loaded <- load_long(data_path, store = store_path)
load_long() creates Parquet files on the first run and reuses them later. These files are already prepared on the workshop machine. loaded contains one table per data type, covering all datasets.



Merge the datasets
Combine the datasets for joint analysis:
merged <- merge_long(loaded)
merge_long() checks for duplicate events (error) and conflicting ASV taxonomy (warning). ASVs with identical sequences are identified across datasets using SBDI ASV IDs.
The resulting merged list contains:

counts: ASV read counts
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomy, one row per ASV
emof: contextual measurements (extended measurement or fact)
events: sample metadata (where, when, how, who)
datasets: dataset metadata
iasvs: ASVs with conflicting taxonomy, or NULL if none

Some tables may not appear in RStudio’s Environment pane. Use names() to see all elements:
names(merged)
For function documentation:
?asvoccur::load_long
?asvoccur::merge_long



Inspect the data
The large tables (counts, asvs and emof) are lazy: their contents are not loaded into R until needed. The smaller tables (events, datasets and iasvs) are ordinary R data frames.
We use familiar dplyr commands through the duckplyr package. For example, count the rows, samples and ASVs:
merged$counts |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    samples = n_distinct(eventID),
    asvs = n_distinct(taxonID)
  ) |>
  as.data.frame()
as.data.frame() tells DuckDB to run the query and returns the result as an ordinary R data frame. By summarising first, we avoid loading the entire table.
Inspect a few rows:
merged$counts |> head(3) |> as.data.frame()
merged$asvs |> select(taxonID, phylum, order, genus, species) |> head(3) |> as.data.frame()
See which contextual measurements are available:
merged$emof |> distinct(measurementType, measurementUnit) |> as.data.frame()



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
Sum ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels:
clades <- sum_clades_long(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
The result has one row per clade and sample, at levels from kingdom (or domain) to species, including otu if available.

raw: read counts
norm: proportion of reads in the sample (relative abundance)

The result is also lazy. To inspect phylum-level counts:
clades |>
  filter(rank == "phylum") |>
  head(3) |>
  as.data.frame()
ASVs missing an annotation at a given level are grouped as Unclassified. Existing annotation names such as unclassified.Acrididae are preserved.
The data are now ready for analysis. In the next steps, we explore sampling locations, taxonomic composition and diversity.

title: 6B. Within-sample diversity (track B: insects)
text:
Examine diversity within each sample — alpha diversity — using the Shannon index, complementing the between-sample comparison in step 5.

Select samples
Extraction methods can affect how many taxa are detected. To avoid mixing methods when comparing habitats, we use only lysate samples that pass the depth and date filters from step 3:
alpha_samples <- events[
  events$depth >= 100000 & !is.na(events$yday) & grepl("lysate", events$eventID),
]
nrow(alpha_samples)
Unlike in the previous analyses, we do not require matched sample pairs.


Subsample to a common depth
Samples with more reads may reveal more rare taxa, affecting diversity estimates. We therefore randomly subsample each to the same number of reads (rarefaction).
As in step 5, we work with clusters rather than individual ASVs:
alpha_ids <- duckdb_tibble(eventID = alpha_samples$eventID, .prudence = "stingy")

alpha_counts <- merged$counts |>
  semi_join(alpha_ids, by = "eventID") |>
  inner_join(clusters, by = "taxonID") |>
  summarise(quant = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(eventID, cluster)) |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = cluster, quant)

set.seed(1)
alpha_rarefied <- el_rrarefy(alpha_counts)
el_rrarefy() works like rrarefy() in vegan. By default, it uses the smallest sample total as the common depth. set.seed() makes the random subsampling reproducible.
Unlike the other ecolongr functions used here, el_rrarefy() loads the data into R, which is manageable for this dataset.


Calculate Shannon diversity
The Shannon index measures both the number of taxa and how evenly their abundances are distributed. Higher values indicate greater within-sample diversity.
shannon <- el_diversity(alpha_rarefied, "shannon")
alpha_samples$shannon <- shannon[alpha_samples$eventID]


Plot Shannon diversity by habitat
plot_shannon <- function() {
  par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1))
  boxplot(alpha_samples$shannon ~ alpha_samples$habitat, las = 2, xlab = "",
          ylab = "Shannon diversity",
          col = habitat_cols[levels(factor(alpha_samples$habitat))])
}

plot_shannon()
Shannon diversity is broadly similar across habitats, with overlapping distributions.
This does not contradict the PCoA results in step 5. Beta diversity describes differences in community composition between samples, while alpha diversity describes diversity within each sample. Habitats can therefore have different communities but similar Shannon diversity.
Consider: Can two habitats have similar Shannon diversity even if they contain very different insect groups? What does this tell us about the difference between alpha and beta diversity?

title: 5A. Community differences (track A: marine plankton)
text:
Compare microbial communities between samples using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).

Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
Bray-Curtis dissimilarity measures differences in taxon abundance between samples, from 0 (identical composition) to 1 (no shared taxa). Both datasets use the same primers, allowing ASV-level comparisons.
vegan expects one row per sample, so we first turn the sparse count matrix into an ordinary matrix with samples as rows:
asv_table <- t(as.matrix(merged$counts))
dim(asv_table)
We then calculate relative abundances to reduce the influence of sequencing depth, and Bray-Curtis dissimilarities between all samples:
asv_shares <- decostand(asv_table, "total")
bray <- vegdist(asv_shares, "bray")
The result is a dist object, ordered to match events.


Run PCoA
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) places samples in a plot based on their dissimilarities. Samples closer together have more similar communities.
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)


Plot PCoA results
We plot each dataset separately, with all samples shown in grey for reference. As in the maps from step 3, colour indicates day of year and point size indicates salinity.
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  layout(matrix(c(1, 2, 3, 4), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE), heights = c(4, 1))
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

  for (dataset in c("2019-2020", "2013")) {
    ix <- events$dataset == dataset
    plot(x, y, col = "grey85", pch = 16, cex = 0.8,
         xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = dataset)
    points(x[ix], y[ix], pch = dataset_pch[dataset], col = "black",
           bg = color_yday[events$yday[ix]], cex = point_size(events$salinity[ix], 0.8, 15))
  }

  par(mar = c(3, 2, 1, 2))
  plot(1:366, rep(1, 366), col = color_yday, pch = "|", cex = 3,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0.9, 1.3))
  axis(1, at = c(1, 182, 366))
  text(183, 1.2, "Day of year")

  plot(c(2, 18, 34), rep(1, 3), pch = 1, cex = 0.8 + c(2, 18, 34) / 15,
       xlim = c(-5, 40), ylim = c(0.9, 1.3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(1, at = c(2, 18, 34))
  text(18, 1.2, "Salinity")
}

plot_pcoa()
The first axis accounts for about a third of the variation and is associated with salinity: samples from the brackish Baltic Sea lie to the left, while those from the saltier Kattegat and Skagerrak lie to the right. Within these groups, the second axis appears to reflect seasonal differences.
The 2013 samples follow a similar pattern to the later samples, supporting comparisons between the datasets, although other differences in sampling and methods may still matter.
Consider: Which appears to be more strongly associated with community composition: salinity or season? What can the PCoA plot tell us, and what can it not tell us?

title: Import and analyse ASV portal data with R
text:
This tutorial covers the main steps for importing and analysing data from the ASV portal in R. You can choose between two tracks, marine plankton and insects, which follow the same analysis steps but use different datasets and approaches to data handling. Choose the one that best matches your interests and experience.

Track A: Marine plankton — traditional R workflow. Analyse 16S metabarcoding data of bacterioplankton from the Baltic Sea, sampled along the salinity gradient from the Bothnian Bay to the Skagerrak in 2013 and 2019–2020. The data are handled as wide, sparse matrices with familiar R tools. A good starting point if you are new to metabarcoding data analysis.
Track B: Insects — working with large datasets. Analyse COI metabarcoding data from the Insect Biome Atlas (IBA), which sampled arthropods with Malaise traps at 200 sites across six habitat types in Sweden, using two extraction protocols (homogenate and lysate). The data are handled as long tables with Parquet and DuckDB, tools for datasets too large to fit comfortably in R’s memory.


Common step

Environment setup — Access the workshop RStudio environment (or run locally), and choose your data



Track A: Marine plankton

Data preparation — Load, merge and aggregate the data as wide matrices
Sample mapping — Map samples and their salinity across the Baltic Sea
Taxonomic composition — Barplots across salinity and months
Community differences (beta diversity) — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Shannon diversity along the salinity gradient



Track B: Insects

Data preparation — Load, merge and aggregate the data as long tables
Sample mapping — Filter, pair and map samples across Sweden and habitat types
Taxonomic composition — Barplots across habitats, months and extraction methods
Community differences (beta diversity) — Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and PCoA
Within-sample diversity (alpha diversity) — Shannon diversity across habitat types

Get started →

title: 2A. Data preparation (track A: marine plankton)
text:
Load and combine the plankton data in wide format, and summarise read counts by taxonomy.

How the data look

ASV read counts can be organised in wide format, with one row per ASV and one column per sample, or in long format, with one row per ASV–sample combination. The tables below show the same read counts in the two formats.


Wide

251






This track uses wide format, which many R packages, such as vegan, work with. Since most counts are zero, we store them in a sparse matrix: not a third format, but a way of storing a matrix that keeps only the non-zero values.



Load the datasets
Load the data from the data_path folder defined in the previous section:
loaded <- load_data(data_path)
load_data() reads the ZIP files and converts the read counts to wide format. loaded contains one list per data type, with one element per dataset.



Merge the datasets
Combine the datasets for joint analysis:
merged <- merge_data(loaded)
names(merged)
merge_data() stops if the same sample occurs in more than one dataset. ASVs with identical sequences are identified across datasets using SBDI ASV IDs.
The resulting merged list contains:

counts: ASV read counts, with one row per ASV and one column per sample
asvs: ASV sequences and taxonomy, one row per ASV
events: sample metadata (where, when, how, who), one row per sample
emof: contextual measurements (extended measurement or fact), one row per sample and one column per measurement
datasets: dataset metadata

The tables are in the same order: the columns of counts follow the rows of events and emof, and the rows of counts follow the rows of asvs.
For function documentation:
?asvoccur::load_data
?asvoccur::merge_data



Inspect the data
counts is the sparse matrix. Check its size (ASVs × samples) and look at a corner of it:
dim(merged$counts)
merged$counts[1:3, 1:2]
The dots are zeros. The other tables are ordinary data frames:
head(merged$asvs[, c("taxonID", "phylum", "class", "genus")], 3)



Aggregate counts by taxonomy
Sum ASV read counts at different taxonomic levels:
clades <- sum_by_clade(merged$counts, merged$asvs)
names(clades$norm)
The result has one matrix per level, from kingdom (or domain) to species, including otu if available. Each matrix has one row per clade and one column per sample.

raw: read counts
norm: proportion of reads in the sample (relative abundance)

To inspect class-level shares in the first two samples:
clades$norm$class[1:3, 1:2]
ASVs missing an annotation at a given level are grouped as Unclassified.
The data are now ready for analysis. In the next steps, we explore sampling locations, taxonomic composition and diversity.

title: 4A. Taxonomic composition (track A: marine plankton)
text:
Compare the relative abundance of plankton groups across salinity and months.

Group samples by salinity
We use the relative abundances in clades$norm from step 2, and group the samples into salinity intervals. Samples without salinity measurements or outside the intervals are excluded from the comparison. The intervals are chosen for the figure, not as a biological classification.
salinity_breaks <- c(0, 3, 6, 12, 20, 35)
events$salinity_class <- cut(events$salinity, salinity_breaks, right = FALSE)
table(events$salinity_class)


Plot taxonomic composition
The function below selects the most abundant taxa at a chosen rank and plots their mean share of reads for each salinity interval and month using ggplot2.
plot_barplots <- function(rank, top_x = 10) {
  keep <- !is.na(events$salinity_class)
  shares <- as.matrix(clades$norm[[rank]][, keep])
  top <- names(sort(rowMeans(shares), decreasing = TRUE))[1:top_x]

  # One row per taxon and sample, then the mean share per salinity interval and month
  composition <- data.frame(
    clade = rep(top, times = sum(keep)),
    salinity_class = rep(events$salinity_class[keep], each = top_x),
    month = rep(events$month[keep], each = top_x),
    share = as.vector(shares[top, ])
  )
  monthly <- aggregate(share ~ clade + salinity_class + month, composition, mean)

  # Reversed levels put the most abundant taxon at the bottom of each bar
  monthly$clade <- factor(monthly$clade, levels = rev(top))
  monthly$month <- factor(monthly$month, levels = 1:12, labels = month.abb)

  mycols <- colorRampPalette(c(
    "#a6cee3", "#1f78b4", "#b2df8a", "#33a02c",
    "#fb9a99", "#e31a1c", "#fdbf6f", "#ff7f00",
    "#cab2d6", "#6a3d9a", "#ffff99", "#b15928"
  ))

  ggplot(monthly, aes(x = month, y = share, fill = clade)) +
    geom_col(colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.2) +
    facet_wrap(~salinity_class, ncol = 1, labeller = label_both) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(mycols(top_x), top), breaks = top, name = rank) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean share of reads") +
    theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
Available ranks are kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species and otu.


Example: plot top classes
Plot the eight most abundant classes:
plot_barplots(rank = "class", top_x = 8)
Each bar shows the mean relative abundance of these classes among samples from a given salinity interval and month.
Bacteroidia and Alphaproteobacteria are common across salinities, while Acidimicrobiia and Actinomycetes are more common in less saline water. Cyanobacteriia increase in summer, and many reads remain Unclassified.
These are shares of sequencing reads, not estimates of cell abundance. Bars may not add up to 100% because only the eight most abundant classes are shown. Empty months indicate that no samples were available in that salinity interval.
Consider: How does community composition vary with salinity and season? Can we separate these effects given the sampling patterns seen in step 3?

title: 3B. Sample mapping (track B: insects)
text:
Explore where and when samples were collected, and which habitats they represent.

Inspect sample metadata
merged$events contains one row per sample, including location, date and environmental information:
events <- merged$events
colnames(events)



Prepare dates
The two datasets store dates as start/end intervals. We extract the start date to calculate month and day of year.
Records containing only a year cannot be assigned a month or day and will be excluded when filtering samples.
event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
events$month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
events$yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)
events$date  <- as.Date(event_start)



Prepare habitat types
The env_local_scale column contains habitat classifications from the Environment Ontology (ENVO).
unique(events$env_local_scale)
We assign shorter labels and colours for plotting:
habitat_map <- c(
  "forested area [ENVO:00000111]"    = "forest",
  "area of cropland [ENVO:01000892]" = "cropland",
  "wetland area [ENVO:00000043]"     = "wetland",
  "grassland area [ENVO:00000106]"   = "grassland",
  "urban biome [ENVO:01000249]"      = "urban",
  "alpine biome [ENVO:01001835]"     = "alpine"
)
events$habitat <- unname(habitat_map[events$env_local_scale])

habitat_cols <- c(
  "forest"    = "#2d6a4f",
  "cropland"  = "#d4a017",
  "wetland"   = "#4895ef",
  "grassland" = "#95d5b2",
  "urban"     = "#adb5bd",
  "alpine"    = "#9b5de5"
)



Filter samples
Samples with very few reads may give unreliable estimates of community composition. We therefore exclude samples with fewer than 100,000 reads, as well as those without a complete date.
First, calculate the total read count per sample:
depth <- merged$counts |>
  summarise(depth = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = eventID) |>
  as.data.frame()

events <- merge(events, depth, by = "eventID")
summary(events$depth)
Then apply the filters:
samples <- events[events$depth >= 100000 & !is.na(events$yday), ]
nrow(samples)
The threshold of 100,000 reads is used for these datasets. Check the depth summary before applying a different threshold to other data.



Match extraction methods
The two datasets use different extraction methods (homogenate and lysate) and differ in sample coverage.
To compare the methods fairly, we retain only site–date combinations represented by both methods. This avoids confounding extraction method with location or season.
samples$method <- sub(":.*", "", samples$eventID)
samples$site_date <- paste(samples$locationID, samples$date)

shared <- Reduce(intersect, split(samples$site_date, samples$method))
samples <- samples[samples$site_date %in% shared, ]
table(samples$method)
We use these matched samples throughout the remaining analyses. Each site–date combination has one sample per extraction method, so paired samples are not independent.



Map samples
Plot the samples by month, coloured by habitat:
plot_monthly_maps <- function() {
  newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")
  par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1), xpd = TRUE)

  for (m in 1:12) {
    in_month <- samples[samples$month == m, ]
    plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(55, 70), asp = 1, main = month.abb[m])
    if (nrow(in_month) > 0) {
      points(in_month$decimalLongitude, in_month$decimalLatitude, pch = 21,
             col = "black", bg = habitat_cols[in_month$habitat], cex = 1.5)
    }
  }

  plot.new()
  legend("left", bty = "n", legend = names(habitat_cols),
         pt.bg = habitat_cols, pch = 21, pt.cex = 1.6, cex = 1.1,
         title = "Habitat")
}

plot_monthly_maps()
Click Zoom in RStudio’s Plots pane for a larger view. Paired samples overlap, and nearby sites may also appear as a single point at this scale.
Consider: Are the samples evenly distributed across Sweden, habitats and seasons? How might this affect the conclusions we can draw?

title: 3A. Sample mapping (track A: marine plankton)
text:
Explore where and when Baltic Sea samples were collected, and how salinity varies.
The two datasets contain 16S metabarcoding data of bacterioplankton from a transect sampled in July 2013 (KTH-2013-Baltic-16S) and monitoring stations sampled in 2019–2020 (PRJEB55296-16S).

Inspect sample metadata
merged$events contains one row per sample. We copy it to an ordinary data frame and label the datasets, using the dataset ID at the start of each eventID:
events <- as.data.frame(merged$events)
dataset_labels <- c("KTH-2013-Baltic-16S" = "2013", "PRJEB55296-16S" = "2019-2020")
events$dataset <- unname(dataset_labels[sub(":.*", "", events$eventID)])
table(events$dataset)



Check primers
Different primers may amplify different parts of the microbial community. We therefore check that both datasets used the same primers before comparing ASVs:
unique(events[c("dataset", "pcr_primer_name_forward", "pcr_primer_name_reverse")])
Both datasets use the same primers.



Prepare dates
Extract the month and day of year from eventDate:
event_start <- lubridate::parse_date_time(
  sub("/.*", "", events$eventDate),
  orders = c("ymd_HMSz", "ymd_HMS", "ymd_HM", "ymd"),
  quiet = TRUE
)
events$month <- lubridate::month(event_start)
events$yday  <- lubridate::yday(event_start)



Extract salinity
Salinity is stored in merged$emof, which has one row per sample and one column per contextual measurement. The two datasets use different names for salinity:
grep("salinity", colnames(merged$emof), value = TRUE)
We take salinity from salinity (psu) for the 2013 samples and from salinity_average (psu) for the 2019–2020 samples. The rows of emof are in the same order as those of events:
events$salinity <- ifelse(events$dataset == "2013",
                          merged$emof$`salinity (psu)`,
                          merged$emof$`salinity_average (psu)`)
summary(events$salinity)
Some samples lack salinity measurements. They are shown with the smallest point size and excluded from later comparisons involving salinity.



Map samples
Plot the samples by month. Point colour indicates day of year, point size indicates salinity, and point shape distinguishes the datasets.
# Point size grows with salinity; missing values get the smallest size
point_size <- function(salinity, base, step) base + ifelse(is.na(salinity), 0, salinity / step)

color_yday <- colorRampPalette(
  c("#2c7fb8", "#addd8e", "#edf8b1", "#fa9fb5", "#2c7fb8")
)(366)
dataset_pch <- c("2013" = 21, "2019-2020" = 22)

plot_maps <- function(dataset) {
  in_dataset <- events[events$dataset == dataset, ]
  newmap <- rworldmap::getMap(resolution = "low")
  par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(2, 2, 3, 1), xpd = TRUE)

  for (m in 1:12) {
    in_month <- in_dataset[in_dataset$month %in% m, ]
    plot(newmap, xlim = c(10, 25), ylim = c(54, 66), asp = 1, main = month.abb[m])
    if (nrow(in_month) > 0) {
      points(in_month$decimalLongitude, in_month$decimalLatitude,
             pch = dataset_pch[dataset], col = "black",
             bg = color_yday[in_month$yday], cex = point_size(in_month$salinity, 1, 20))
    }
  }

  plot(1:366, rep(1, 366), col = color_yday, pch = "|", cex = 3,
       axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(0.9, 1.3))
  axis(1, at = c(1, 182, 366))
  text(183, 1.2, "Day of year", cex = 1.2)

  plot(c(2, 18, 34), rep(1, 3), pch = 1, cex = 1 + c(2, 18, 34) / 20,
       xlim = c(-5, 40), ylim = c(0.9, 1.3), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  axis(1, at = c(2, 18, 34))
  text(18, 1.2, "Salinity", cex = 1.2)
}

plot_maps("2019-2020")
Use the same function to map the 2013 transect:
plot_maps("2013")
Click Zoom in RStudio’s Plots pane for a larger view.
Consider: How do the sampling locations and seasons differ between the two datasets? What patterns do you see in salinity, and how might these differences affect comparisons of microbial communities?

title: 6A. Within-sample diversity (track A: marine plankton)
text:
Examine diversity within each sample — alpha diversity — using the Shannon index, and how it varies with salinity.

Subsample to a common depth
Samples with more reads may reveal more rare taxa, affecting diversity estimates. We therefore randomly subsample each to the same number of reads (rarefaction). We reuse asv_table from step 5.
First, inspect the sequencing depth (total reads) of the samples:
depth <- rowSums(asv_table)
summary(depth)
sort(depth)[1:10]  # the shallowest samples
One sample has only 20 reads, and a few others have fewer than 10,000. Rarefying to the minimum depth would discard almost all information, so we choose 10,000 reads instead, and leave out the samples with fewer reads. These samples will have no Shannon value.
set.seed(1)
asv_rarefied <- rrarefy(asv_table[depth >= 10000, ], 10000)
set.seed() makes the random subsampling reproducible.


Calculate Shannon diversity
The Shannon index measures both the number of ASVs and how evenly their abundances are distributed. Higher values indicate greater within-sample diversity.
shannon <- diversity(asv_rarefied, "shannon")
events$shannon <- shannon[events$eventID]


Plot Shannon diversity against salinity
plot_shannon <- function() {
  par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
  plot(events$salinity, events$shannon,
       pch = dataset_pch[events$dataset], bg = color_yday[events$yday],
       xlab = "Salinity", ylab = "Shannon diversity")
  legend("bottomright", bty = "n", pch = dataset_pch, legend = names(dataset_pch))
}

plot_shannon()
Shannon diversity shows no clear trend with salinity. Instead, it appears to vary more with season, with winter samples (blue) generally showing higher diversity than summer samples.
This complements the PCoA results in step 5: salinity is associated with differences in which bacteria are present (beta diversity), but not with a simple change in within-sample diversity (alpha diversity).
Consider: How can salinity be associated with community composition without showing a clear relationship with Shannon diversity?

title: SMN hands-on workshop in Uppsala
text:
Part of the first in-person Swedish Metabarcoding Network (SMN) meeting.
In this hands-on workshop, we explore metabarcoding data from raw sequencing reads to biodiversity patterns. We process reads into ASVs using nf-core/ampliseq, then analyse data from the ASV portal in R with asvoccur and ecolongr. These tools are developed by, or with contributions from, the Swedish Biodiversity Data Infrastructure (SBDI).

title: 5B. Community differences (track B: insects)
text:
Compare insect communities between samples using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA).
We use counts_selected from step 4, containing the samples selected in step 3.

Aggregate ASVs to clusters
Most pairs of samples share few ASVs, making ASV-level comparisons less informative. The IBA datasets include project-specific cluster assignments in associatedSequences, allowing us to compare communities at cluster level instead.
We retrieve the cluster assignments from loaded, since they are specific to each dataset and are not retained by merge_long():
clusters <- loaded$asvs |> distinct(taxonID, cluster = associatedSequences)

cluster_counts <- counts_selected |>
  inner_join(clusters, by = "taxonID") |>
  summarise(quant = sum(organismQuantity, na.rm = TRUE), .by = c(eventID, cluster)) |>
  transmute(sample = eventID, taxon = cluster, quant)
The column names sample, taxon and quant are expected by ecolongr. cluster_counts is still a lazy query.


Calculate Bray-Curtis dissimilarity
Bray-Curtis measures differences in taxon abundance between samples, from 0 (identical composition) to 1 (no shared taxa).
We calculate relative abundances to reduce the influence of sequencing depth, then calculate dissimilarities:
bray <- cluster_counts |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = samples$eventID)
These functions work like decostand() and vegdist() in vegan, but process the large table without loading it into R. The result is an ordinary dist object, ordered to match samples.


Run PCoA
Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) places samples in a plot based on their dissimilarities. Samples closer together have more similar communities.
pcoa <- cmdscale(bray, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

# Share of the positive eigenvalues held by each of the first two axes
axis_share <- pcoa$eig[1:2] / sum(pcoa$eig[pcoa$eig > 0])
round(100 * axis_share, 1)
PCoA requires the full dissimilarity matrix in memory, which can become demanding for very large datasets.


Prepare colour scales
We reuse habitat_cols from step 3 and define colours for sampling date, latitude and extraction method:
ramp <- colorRampPalette(rev(c(
  "#D73027", "#FC8D59", "#FEE090", "#FFFFBF", "#E0F3F8", "#91BFDB", "#4575B4"
)))

yday_range <- min(samples$yday):max(samples$yday)
color_yday <- ramp(length(yday_range))
yday_index <- samples$yday - min(yday_range) + 1

lat_range <- floor(min(samples$decimalLatitude)):ceiling(max(samples$decimalLatitude))
color_lat <- ramp(length(lat_range))
lat_index <- round(samples$decimalLatitude) - min(lat_range) + 1

method_cols <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "#e76f51",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "#2a9d8f"
)
method_labs <- c(
  IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE = "homogenate",
  IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE = "lysate"
)
Define legend labels for latitude and sampling month:
lat_ticks <- seq(ceiling(min(lat_range) / 2) * 2, max(lat_range), by = 2)

month_ticks  <- sort(tapply(samples$yday, samples$month, min))
month_labels <- month.abb[as.integer(names(month_ticks))]


Plot PCoA results
We plot the same PCoA four times, colouring samples by date, habitat, latitude and extraction method:
plot_pcoa <- function() {
  xlab <- paste0("PC1 (", round(100 * axis_share[1]), "%)")
  ylab <- paste0("PC2 (", round(100 * axis_share[2]), "%)")
  x <- pcoa$points[, 1]
  y <- pcoa$points[, 2]

  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 6), xpd = TRUE)

  # Panel: colour by year-day
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_yday[yday_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by year-day")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_yday[month_ticks - min(yday_range) + 1],
         legend = month_labels)

  # Panel: colour by habitat
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = habitat_cols[samples$habitat], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by habitat")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = habitat_cols, legend = names(habitat_cols))

  # Panel: colour by latitude
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = color_lat[lat_index], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by latitude")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = color_lat[lat_ticks - min(lat_range) + 1],
         legend = lat_ticks)

  # Panel: colour by extraction method
  plot(x, y, col = "black", bg = method_cols[samples$method], pch = 21, cex = 1,
       xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, main = "Colour by extraction method")
  legend("bottomleft", bty = "n", pch = 19, cex = 1, inset = c(1, 0),
         col = method_cols, legend = method_labs)
}

plot_pcoa()
The first two axes together account for only about 10% of the variation, so the plots show only part of the differences among communities.
Nevertheless, patterns are visible: northern samples tend to group in one direction, forest samples spread along the first axis, and spring samples form a distinct tail. Homogenate and lysate samples overlap considerably but are not completely mixed; the spring tail, for example, consists mainly of homogenate samples.
Consider: Which factors appear to be associated with community composition? How does the low percentage represented by the first two axes affect our interpretation?

title: 1. Environment setup
text:
Workshop RStudio (recommended)
During the workshop, we use RStudio Server on a virtual machine in PDC Cloud. Log in with the username and password you receive at the workshop:
RStudio Server
All packages and datasets are already prepared, so no installation or downloading is needed.






Note



The machine is shared and will shut down after the workshop.

Avoid creating unnecessary large objects.
If you want to keep your code, save it as an R script and download it before you leave (Files → More → Export).




Choose your track
Choose the track you want to follow. The overview describes the tracks. Set the paths to the example data and check that the ZIP files are available.

Track A: Marine planktonTrack B: Insects


data_path <- "/srv/course-data/plankton"
list.files(data_path)
You should see two ZIP files (16S).


data_path  <- "/srv/course-data/insects"
store_path <- "/srv/course-store/insects"
list.files(data_path)
You should see two ZIP files (IBA_CO1).

title: 1. Environment setup
text:
Check required packages
Load the packages used in your track:

Track A: Marine planktonTrack B: Insects


library(asvoccur)
library(vegan)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
If the packages load without errors and your data files are listed, you are ready for the next step.


library(asvoccur)
library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)
library(rworldmap)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)
If the packages load without errors and your data files are listed, you are ready for the next step.



Running locally? Click and follow the installation instructions below before continuing.






NoteRunning the tutorial locally (optional)





You can also run the tutorial on your own computer, but you will need to install R, the required packages and download the example data.

Install R and packages
Install R and RStudio.
For the insect track, you also need tools for compiling R packages because ecolongr contains C++ code:

macOS: Run xcode-select --install in Terminal.
Windows: Install Rtools for your R version.
Linux: Install build-essential and r-base-dev (or equivalent).

Install the packages in R:
install.packages(c(
  "remotes", "duckplyr", "vegan",
  "rworldmap", "lubridate", "ggplot2"
))

remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/asvoccur@v1.3.0")
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/ecolongr@0.2.2")
Load the packages using the code above. Check the versions:
packageVersion("asvoccur")  # 1.3.0
packageVersion("ecolongr")  # 0.2.2


Download example data

Open the ASV portal and click DOWNLOAD.
Sign in with Google or GitHub, or create an SBDI account.
Download the two datasets for your track:

Marine plankton: KTH-2013-Baltic-16S and PRJEB55296-16S
Insects: IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE and IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE

Place the two ZIP files in a folder for your track. Do not unzip them.

For example:
course-data/
└── insects/
    ├── IBA_CO1_homogenate_2019_SE.zip
    └── IBA_CO1_lysate_2019_SE.zip


Set data paths
Set the path to your downloaded ZIP files. For the insect track, also set a folder where processed data will be stored:
data_path  <- "local/path/to/course-data/insects"
store_path <- "local/path/to/course-store/insects"
list.files(data_path)
Adjust the paths for your computer and chosen track. The store folder will be created during data preparation.
If the two ZIP files are listed, you are ready to continue with track A or track B.
